title: Diwali, festival of lights
hook: the festival of lights, kept by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, each for their own reasons
tomorrow: Buddhism: the man under the tree

segments.voice: Yesterday, puja, the lamp and the flower. Your line was one flame. Day two hundred thirty-eight, the last day of our Hindu visit.

A clay lamp no bigger than a palm: a cotton wick, a spoon of oil. Now set one on every windowsill, every rooftop, every doorstep in a city. Colored powder patterns on the ground at the front door. Sweets carried house to house in boxes. Fireworks cracking over the rooftops until late. New clothes. Family on the phone from three continents. All of it on a night with no moon at all. Our Hindu visit ends with its festival of lamps: Diwali, the festival of lights.
screen: `A CLAY LAMP THE SIZE OF A PALM.` → `A NIGHT WITH NO MOON.` → `DIWALI.`

segments.voice: Diwali comes from the Sanskrit Deepavali, a row of lamps. It falls on a new moon night in autumn, and in many places the celebration runs over several days. But why light the lamps? That depends on who you ask. In much of north India, Hindus tell that Diwali remembers the god Rama coming home to his city, Ayodhya, after fourteen years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana, with the people lighting lamps to welcome him. Hindu families also worship the goddess Lakshmi that night, asking her blessing on home and work. In parts of south India, the festival remembers Krishna's defeat of the demon Narakasura. In Bengal, the same night belongs to the goddess Kali. And it isn't only Hindu. Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release, remembering the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, freed from imprisonment in Gwalior Fort, and the Golden Temple in Amritsar blazes with lights. Jains remember the night Mahavira, in their tradition the twenty-fourth great teacher, attained final liberation; they light lamps because, as they tell it, the light of his wisdom had gone out of the world. Same night, same lamps, different stories. Each tradition keeps its own, and none needs the others' to make sense. What they share is the picture: light against the dark. And that closes our Hindu week. Dharma. You are that. The act, not the fruit. Namaste. Puja. And now, a row of lamps.
screen: `DEEPAVALI: A ROW OF LAMPS.` · `RAMA COMES HOME; LAKSHMI.` · `SIKHS: BANDI CHHOR DIVAS.` · `JAINS: MAHAVIRA'S LIBERATION.` · then, large: `LIGHT OVER DARK.`

segments.voice: If it's safe, set a candle or a small light where it can be seen from outside; if not, picture a single clay lamp on a windowsill at night. Think of one darkness near you: a worry, a grief, someone having a hard month. Don't fix it; just let the small flame sit beside it.
Diwali. The festival of lights: a row of lamps kept by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains on the same night, each for their own reasons. Today's word.
Your line: light over dark. Thank you for being a good guest this week. On to Buddhism tomorrow.
